steps.page: Feature tags: one shared checklist per kind of app
steps.intro: Your idea: instead of everyone re-wording 'X is missing live editing', each kind of app gets a short checklist, and every project gets a yes / partly / no per item.

steps.headline: Should each group get a short, reusable checklist of the features people care about?
steps.today: Gaps are free-text notes like 'Encrypted; simpler formatting than Word', one per project, worded differently each time.
steps.problem: You can't tell 'nothing open does live co-editing' from 'LibreOffice lacks live co-editing', and the same complaint gets re-written by every person.
steps.proposal: Documents would get about 6 items: Live co-editing · Opens Word files exactly · Comments & suggested edits · Works offline · Phone app · Free hosted option. Each project shows yes / partly / no. An item where every project says no becomes 'Missing everywhere' on the gaps page automatically. Many items are shared across groups (Phone app, Works offline, End-to-end encrypted), so they're written once.

steps.headline: How should each project answer a checklist item?
steps.problem: Too few answers hide real differences; too many become guesswork.

options.label: Yes / partly / no
pros: Captures 'it sort of works' (LibreOffice opens Word files, but layouts can shift).
Still easy to scan.
cons: 'Partly' needs a short note to be useful.

options.label: Yes / no
pros: The simplest to read and fill in.
cons: Forces hard calls where support is half-there.

steps.headline: Who fills in the checklists at the start?
steps.today: Listings were drafted with AI help and checked by mods.
steps.problem: About 470 projects × about 6 items is roughly 2,800 answers: too many for two mods by hand.

options.label: AI draft, clearly marked
pros: Every project has answers on day one.
Uses the same 'drafted with AI assistance' label as the rest of the listing, which disappears once a developer claims the page.
cons: Some answers will be wrong until someone corrects them.

options.label: Only people fill them
pros: Every answer had human eyes.
cons: Mostly empty for months.

steps.headline: Who can change or correct an answer?
steps.today: Corrections go through GitHub forms to mods.
steps.problem: Answers go stale as projects add features; mods can't track them all.

options.label: The project's developer
pros: They know best; it updates at once on a claimed page.
cons: Developers may be generous to themselves; others can still dispute.

options.label: Signed-in users confirm or dispute
pros: One tap: 'Is this right? Yes / No'. Enough 'No' flags it for a mod.
No re-wording the same complaint.
cons: Needs the 14-day account rule to stop fake votes.

options.label: Mods
pros: Final say on disputes.
cons: Their time.

steps.headline: Where should the checklist show up?
steps.problem: A checklist only helps if people can use it to choose and builders can see what's missing.
steps.proposal: Tick every place you want it.

options.label: 'Must have' filter chips
pros: Tap 'Live co-editing' and only projects that do it stay on the group page.
cons: One more row of chips above the list.

options.label: A compare table
pros: Every project and every item side by side; great for choosing between three.
cons: Wide; on phones it scrolls sideways or folds.

options.label: On each card
pros: A quiet line like 'Live co-editing · No phone app'.
cons: Cards get busier, which you just asked me to avoid; I'd keep it to the explainer pop-up.

options.label: 'Missing everywhere' on gaps
pros: Builders see exactly which feature no open app has, with how many people want it.
cons: None worth noting.

steps.headline: What happens to the free-text 'What's missing' boards?
steps.today: People post free-text notes and vote 'Me too'.
steps.problem: With checklists, most notes would repeat a checklist item.
steps.proposal: Three ways to fit them together.

options.label: Notes become proposals
pros: A note proposes a NEW checklist item ('Track changes'); once a mod adds it, its votes carry over as 'I want this'.
No duplicates; discussion still possible.
cons: A bit more structure for people to understand.

options.label: Keep both separately
pros: Nothing changes for posting.
cons: Two places for the same complaint.

options.label: Replace the boards
pros: Simplest page.
cons: No room for things that aren't a feature (pricing, community, tone).

steps.intro: Real examples from our list: CapRover welcomes AI code. Nextcloud wants it declared with an 'Assisted-by' line. Zulip wants you to fully understand and test it. goatcounter accepts none. Syncthing allows AI code but not AI-written issues.

steps.headline: Which set of short labels reads most clearly?
steps.today: Nothing says how a project feels about AI-assisted help.
steps.problem: The last three labels were vague, and they couldn't show partial rules like 'code yes, issues no'.
steps.proposal: Each set shows only when the project has a written rule, and tapping it opens the details (next question).

options.label: Plain sentences
options.summary: 'AI-assisted code welcome' · 'AI-assisted code: say you used AI' · 'AI-assisted code: only if you fully understand it' · 'Hand-written code only' · 'Has AI rules: see details'
pros: Says exactly what's allowed.
The last one covers partial rules without cramming them in.
cons: Longer chips.

options.label: Three short pills
pros: Shortest and fastest to scan.
cons: 'AI-friendly' is vague; partial rules get squeezed into one of three.

options.label: Two facts
options.summary: 'AI code: welcome / say so / no' and 'AI issues & reports: welcome / no'
pros: Shows the common 'code yes, issues no' split directly.
cons: Two chips per project.

steps.path: The pop-up that opens from the label
steps.headline: What should the contribution details pop-up show?
steps.today: 'How to help' links the contributing guide and beginner tasks.
steps.problem: People need the specifics before showing up: what's allowed, how to disclose, how to start.
steps.proposal: Tick what belongs in it. Each line is only shown when known.

options.label: Their own words
pros: The project's exact sentence with a link, so nothing is our paraphrase.
cons: None worth noting.

options.label: How to disclose
pros: e.g. 'add an Assisted-by line to your commit' or 'tick the AI box on the pull-request form'.
cons: Only some projects say.

options.label: What it covers
pros: Code / documentation / issues & bug reports / beginner tasks, each allowed or not.
cons: Needs a mod to read the rule carefully.

options.label: Outside help in general
pros: 'Welcomes pull requests' or 'open an issue first' or 'not accepting outside code'.
cons: None worth noting.

options.label: Where to start
pros: Beginner-task and help-wanted counts, plugin docs, contributing guide (what 'How to help' has now).
cons: None worth noting.

options.label: Legal sign-off
pros: Whether they need a sign-off line or a contributor agreement, and that an AI can't sign it for you.
cons: A bit technical for most visitors.

steps.headline: Who sets these labels?
steps.today: Our robot can find and quote the rule; it can't reliably judge what it means.
steps.problem: A wrong label either scares away welcome helpers or sends AI code to a project that refuses it.
steps.proposal: The robot quotes, then someone picks the label.

options.label: Mods, then developers
pros: Mods label the 97 projects that mention AI (about a click each); developers who claim their page can change it.
cons: Mod time up front.

options.label: AI draft, marked
pros: No mod time; same 'drafted with AI' label as other listing facts.
cons: Our scan showed simple matching gets this wrong often; an AI reading the full rule does better, but still errs.
